speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GRANTS TO NATIONAL COUNCIL AND P.E.I. MEMORIAL FOUNDATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two announcements I should like to make in connection with preparations for the observance of the one hundredth anniversary of confederation. The first has to do with the Canadian centenary council, which is holding its annual meeting today and tomorrow. It has associated with it some 160 national associations, either directly or by way of affiliation. The council was established to stimulate interest and participation on the part of the general public in the preparations for the observance of the centennial of confederation.
I wish now to inform the house that, subject to the approval by parliament of the moneys involved, the government will make a grant under the National Centennial Act in the amount of $25,000 early in the fiscal year 1962-63 to assist the Canadian centenary council in its activities. Active participation by citizens everywhere in the country is essential if Canadians are to make the centennial one of the truly significant events in their history.
Second, subject also to the approval by parliament of the funds involved, an order in council will be passed early in the next fiscal year to provide an interim grant of $250,000 to the organization known as the fathers of confederation memorial citizens foundation to enable architectural work to be done in connection with the memorial buildings to be erected in Charlottetown by the foundation to commemorate the conference there in 1864. In addition there will be a grant, inclusive of the above interim grant, in the amount of one half the construction costs of the buildings in question, but not exceeding a total grant of $2.8 million.
It will be a condition of the main grant that the foundation shall not award a contract for the construction of the buildings until it has satisfied the appropriate officers of the federal
government that the foundation possesses sufficient funds, including the grant, to cover the full cost of construction of the buildings in question.

subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT "PRIVATE AND PUBLIC INVESTMENT IN CANADA  OUTLOOK 1962"

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT "PRIVATE AND PUBLIC INVESTMENT IN CANADA  OUTLOOK 1962"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am tabling today the report entitled "Private and Public Investment in Canada-Outlook 1962" which summarizes the results of a recent survey of capital spending intentions. The survey, which is conducted annually, is designed to cover anticipated outlays for new plant and equipment, institutional and government facilities and housing.

Canadian Economy
Capital expenditure plans for all sectors of the economy, as outlined in this report, involve total outlays in 1962 of $8.6 billion. This is 6 per cent above the $8.1 billion actually spent last year. Higher capital spending is indicated for each of the major sectors of the economy, with business investment up 2 per cent, residential construction up 4 per cent and institutional and public building up 16 per cent.
Within the business area most of the added strength will be in key commodity producing industries. Capital outlays in manufacturing are expected to increase by 16 per cent, mainly as a result of expanded programs in primary iron and steel, non-ferrous metal processing and petroleum refining. Other areas of business where plans call for significantly larger capital outlays in 1962 include iron ore and non-ferrous metal mining, electric power and communications, and retail trade. Less will be spent in 1962 in pipe line and gas processing plant construction, new office building and in acquiring equipment for the commercial airlines, unusually large programs having been implemented in these fields last year.
The major factor contributing to larger outlays in the area of institutional and public investment is the greatly expanded program of technical school construction which has been made possible through extensive financial assistance by the federal government. Significant increases are also indicated in anticipated outlays for the construction of university and hospital buildings and for federal, provincial and municipal government projects.
Present spending intentions call for a higher level of investment in 1962 in eight of the ten provinces. Only in Alberta and British Columbia, where very large programs of pipe line construction were completed last year, is a lower level of capital spending anticipated.
A capital expenditure program of the size indicated will reinforce the expansion in general activity now under way in Canada. Higher outlays for both new construction and new machinery and equipment will mean increased activity in the construction and related trades and in equipment producing industries. The results of the survey show also that a continuing high proportion of the national product is being devoted to the renewal and expansion of capital facilities.
The two copies I am tabling have been printed in English, which has been the custom over the years. However, I am also having copies printed in French, and they will be made available very shortly.

speechtext:
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his good wishes in respect of my trip to Geneva, which I plan to start on Monday.
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition asked a question about the interrelationship between working out an agreement on a nuclear test ban and general disarmament negotiations, and I dealt with the question at that time. There is nothing further that I can add today.
For a number of weeks a very intensive study has been conducted by the five western powers, including Canada, which participated in the 10 nation disarmament committee negotiations in 1960. The plan which was proposed by President Kennedy to the United Nations last September remains the basic western approach to the disarmament negotiations and many parts of that plan were proposed in the first place by Canada. Others, of course, were proposed by other members of the group of five. A genuine effort has been made by the five western nations to work out a disarmament proposal which will

go as far as possible to meet the suggestions of the five communist nations. I do not think any one of the western five is being inflexible. As negotiations proceed, changes may have to be made in the western proposals.
As the hon. member knows, Canada has taken the position that it would be a good thing to have countries added to the group of 10 for these new negotiations. That has been done, with India and Burma being added from Asia; Sweden from Europe; the United Arab Republic, Nigeria and Ethiopia from Africa; and Mexico and Brazil from Latin America. We think the fact that these eight other countries are participating may help to prevent the negotiations from being deadlocked. Of course no one can tell just what will be the actual result of the negotiations. However, we think it is helpful to have these other eight nations participating. They too have been doing a great deal in the way of preparatory work for the negotiations. We have been in touch with most of them and, as a matter of fact, have worked quite closely with some of them at the United Nations over a long period in connection with this question of disarmament.
The negotiations will probably take some time. As the house knows, they are opening at the foreign ministers level. However, I would expect that before very long the negotiators will get down to the actual business of trying to work out terms of a treaty. I would hope that would be the course followed rather than that of having a whole series of speeches. Later on when some progress has been made, or even if no progress is made, it is possible that the heads of state will meet in Geneva. That matter, of course, has not yet been settled. However, a report must be made to the United Nations disarmament commission before the first day of June. I think we can expect that there may be a meeting of the heads of state before the expiration of that time.
I am very hopeful that it will be possible to achieve results as, of course, not only is there the question of reducing arms but also of preventing the development of more deadly weapons, something which I think is even more serious than the problem of cutting down armaments which at present exist. It seems to me that this disarmament conference in Geneva is of vital importance not only to Canada but to the whole world.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE BETWEEN MATANE AND STE. ANNE DES MONTS, QUE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the other day I had almost exhausted the time allotted to me for remarks upon this bill. There are a number of further points I wish to make in connection with this rail line and why we in this group are very sceptical about the whole proposal. The first point I should like to make today is taken from the report of the royal commission on transportation, volume 2. The commission's views on the provision of new rail facilities are expressed on page 145, and it seems to me that they should be put on the record in relation to the project now before us. The report reads as follows:
As has been Indicated previously. Canada will continue to require new rail lines. The expected economic developments, particularly in mineral and forest products, will require the transportation of large tonnages at low cost. Rail transport will play a vital role in these developments. Such developments will he of great benefit to Canada and should at the same time improve the financial position of the railways.
If I may interpolate here, it seems to me that there is no guarantee or even prospect of a large tonnage of either mineral or forest products on the railway in question so far as the evidence produced by the minister is concerned. The commission goes on to say:
Parliament should assure itself that any proposal for a new line is economically sound before approving it. The commission notes that this has in recent years been the policy that parliament has followed. We heartily approve this procedure. This is not to say that parliament should not under certain circumstances authorize construction of lines for developmental purposes when the immediate revenue cannot be expected to meet all costs. Under these circumstances, the government should be prepared to meet the deficit from public funds and not place the burden on other shippers. We have earlier recommended that the burden of existing uneconomic lines be removed from the shipper. Consequently, we cannot do otherwise than state that new lines should not become a burden. However, it is unlikely that the building of any substantial number of developmental lines will be required in the future.
I should like the minister to note this.
In general it may well be that the provision of road or air transport as the initial transport in new areas is the best procedure to follow.
I interpolate here that the area in question already has an efficient system of road transport and, as the commission points out repeatedly, wherever you have trucking you tend to have efficient competition because it is the kind of field that an entrepreneur can get into fairly cheaply and reasonably. It seems to me that the point of the commission,


that the provision of road or air transport as the initial transport is the best procedure to follow, has been made so far as this area is concerned, and we have no guarantee or indication of those high volume tonnage prospects in forest and mineral products that the commission suggests should be the main reason for putting in a branch line. The commission goes on to say:
The commission has no need to make specific recommendations on building new rail facilities. Each such facility will require the approval of parliament and at that time parliament will have an opportunity to assure itself that the scheme is economically sound.
Have we had any assurance that this scheme is economically sound? I should like hon. members to look at the figure of $14 million as the estimated total cost and the maximum figure of $250,000 as the estimated operating reveune in the first year or years. The Canadian Pacific Railway is one of the few railways in Canada that makes some kind of a profit and pays a dividend, and anyone who owns Canadian Pacific shares knows that in recent years the railway has not earned over 4 per cent. Let us assume that Canadian National Railways can make a profit on this line with operating revenue of $250,000 a year. If it even matches Canadian Pacific's profit on operating revenue, what will the figure amount to? It will probably amount to $12,000 a year. That is the likely profit prospect based on an operating revenue of $250,000 a year. How then can they possibly come anywhere near meeting the capital investment cost of $14 million? I suggest that we simply have not had from the minister or his officials any indication of the economic feasibility of this line.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm, in a friendly way, said that we should call this line the Belzile-English line. I thought it was a pleasant remark. However, I wonder if these two gentlemen are worth respectively, in these terms, $7 million each. Here we have a situation where to develop an area the sum of $14 million is going to be expended, and we can hardly see any economic justification for that expenditure.
Now, I think any members of this house looking at the regions of the country that have fallen behind in economic growth, want to see national resources developed to help them. I think, for example, the sympathy for the maritimes in the rest of the country is enormous in this regard. I would assume that Gaspe has the same difficulties, if not compounded. In this sense we are very strongly for national aid going to this area to improve the economy. However, the particular means

that has been taken to accomplish this purpose, it seems to me will do very little and cost a great deal. The sum of $14 million is substantial enough that, applied in another way, it would mean a subsidy to every individual in that area, according to the population figures, of almost $200.

He would not change his mind but his outlook would be different.
Mr. Chairman, all hon. members feel very strongly about the construction of that line. I know that every one of us, including members


of the opposition who have received the visits of numerous delegations and who have considered the problem, agree that the Gaspe peninsula will finally be developed.
I may not have the knowledge of the hon. member for Port Arthur, but I know full well, for instance, that there is a mine in operation in the Gaspe area, the Gaspe Copper Mines in Murdochville. I am sure that the owners of that mine will be glad to hear that a railroad will be built in the district. Indeed, a delegation from Murdochville came to see me in that connection and they asked me to support the project.
I am aware of the fact that at present those people have to transport the ore by truck over a distance of 65 miles to ship it by rail. Those additional costs paralyse the future development of the Gaspe peninsula, Mr. Chairman.
We also have in the district, the Federal Metals Company; its president, Mr. Pierre Beauchemin, is also president of the East Sullivan Gold Mine Company. That mine is as rich as that of the Gaspe Copper Mines and its president is willing to spend millions to operate it but he clearly stated, when he accompanied a delegation to Ottawa, that he will not spend a red cent on the mine as long as there is no railroad. I cannot blame him. It does not make sense to transport ore by truck from that part of Gaspe North, back of Ste. Anne des Monts, to Matane, then put it on board a privately operated train up to Mont Joli and from there on board a C.N.R. train- to Montreal or the United States.
We cannot urge these people to spend millions of dollars in the Gaspe peninsula without first providing them with adequate means of communication.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to see trucking companies take the ore from the Gaspe mines and try to carry it to the United States or elsewhere over the roads in this area. I should like to see that. I have yet to see them do it. I know that trucks cannot undertake such a job, because they cannot carry enough of the ore taken from our mines.
The hon. member for Port Arthur said that he fails to see why we ought to spend millions on a railway line in that part of Gaspe. It is very easy to come here and talk about expenditures and of this and that. But I think that if the hon. member had any love for the province of Quebec and also for the Gaspe peninsula, he would have no objection, for I believe that, in its whole history, this

is the only substantial amount Gaspe has ever received. And yet, it was discovered in 1534. It seems to me that the hon. member for Port Arthur is in no position to come to us and criticize the government for spending the sum of $16 million on a railway.
Mr. Chairman, let me point out that this sum of $16 million in not as much as it seems, because, instead of paying unemployment insurance benefits as we do now, we will be giving work to our people, therefore that it will be a good investment for the government of Canada.
The hon. member for Port Arthur dealt only with pulpwood, quoting certain figures on the quantity of this product being shipped from that district. If I asked him where pulp-wood is cut in the Gaspe area, he would be quite puzzled.
Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that statistics show that exactly 412,145 cords of pulpwood were cut in the Gaspe peninsula. Those statistics have been worked out and if the hon. member for Port Arthur wants more information, I am willing to spend a half hour with him to explain the situation, inasmuch as he can understand, of course.
Mr. Chairman, let us consider the weight of a cord of wood. A cord of dry wood, if I am not mistaken, weighs about 3,000 pounds. If he wants to know how many tons, he can figure it out for himself.
Of course, before one can discuss that matter, he must know the difference between pulpwood and lumber.
The hon. member for Port Arthur said nothing about the Gaspe lumber industry. However, it is one of the main industries of that region. The only company, the James Richardson Company, with Mr. James Russell as chairman has cut down and sawn 26 million fbm of lumber last year. That is only one company and it has 600 employees.
Mr. Chairman, reference was made to water hauling. Well, I am not saying that ships are not useful. But suppose, for instance, you operate a mill in the Gaspe peninsula and you cut 26 million feet of lumber, are you going to keep your employees on the payroll all year round, knowing that water hauling is in operation only five or six months and that you cannot ship by boat the rest of the year? In such a case, you will wait until the next year to ship your lumber. If the hon. member for Port Arthur had come in my district even two weeks ago, he would have seen the condition of the roads, especially after the rains
Canadian National Railways we had, which made them very slippery and very hazardous for trucking over long hauls because sawn lumber is now being shipped to Montreal. When you think that it has to be carried by truck to Matane, and from there by a private railway to Mont Joli and then transferred to the C.N.R., you realize that it is costly and that the people in the area are unable to compete on the Montreal market.
At the present time, those engaged in cutting pulpwood in our district are earning less than lumbermen in other parts of the country. It is easy to understand. That wood has to be transported by truck to the railroad, which is for them more costly than it is for those whose logging operations are located in the vicinity of a railway line and who can have their wood shipped direct to Montreal, Quebec city or elsewhere.
In the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, the hon. member asked some questions as to the economic aspect of the project. And yet, if he had taken the trouble to read my speech, he would have found that I had put a letter on record dealing with that subject. It was not a letter written by myself but a letter from the East Sullivan Mines Limited to Mr. Roland Gagnon.
Incidentally, I wish to point out to the house that there are only four smelters in Canada and that the Gaspe Peninsula is fortunate in having one at Murdochville. Here is what the secretary treasurer of the East Sullivan Mines said about the smelter in the Gaspe peninsula which will surely know an extraordinary development:
Further to our telephone conversation, I am glad to confirm the following information:
Solbec Copper Mines Limited is a new subsidiary which is developing a copper and zinc mine in the Black lake area, in the eastern townships. The estimated copper production will be close to 20,000 tons of concentrate per year.
We are aware that the smelter of Gaspe Copper would be a proper place to treat our ores, if that plant were not completely isolated due to the lack of communication facilities. We find it unfortunate for the Gaspe peninsula as well as for the eastern part of the province of Quebec that lack of communication facilities forces us, as it were, to have our concentrates treated outside the country, namely in Europe or in the United States.
Mr. Chairman, something has to be done to improve that situation. As a matter of fact, the president of the East Sullivan Mines Limited, says that he is ready to ship concentrates to Gaspe to have them treated. Furthermore, the Federal Metals Corporation is ready to start developing its mine as soon as the railroad is constructed.

Canadian National Railways
Mr. Chairman, I have looked into all the representations made in favour of the construction of that branch line, under the Liberal administration as well as under the present administration. I admit that the situation 20 or 25 years ago was not what it is today; we must recognize that it is only since 1952 that the development of the Gaspe Copper Mines has revealed the huge resources of the Gaspe peninsula.
Now, if you travel from Montreal to Gaspe South, you take the train for Nova Scotia or New Brunswick; when you reach Matapedia, the train for the maritimes, the Ocean Limited, continues on its way; you transfer at Matapedia and you go past Perce to reach the tip of Gaspe. Please note that this situation has existed for almost a hundred years, although the region of Gaspe South does not know the mining development of Gaspe North, because there is not any mine in Gaspe South. And yet, that railway line has always been operated to the benefit of the southern region of the Gaspe peninsula.
On the other hand, when we ask for the construction of a railway line from Gaspe to Matane, that is a distance of approximately 160 or 165 miles, and we are granted a line running for 57 miles only, in order to promote the industrial and mining development of the northern region of the Gaspe peninsula, there is an uproar. Why? Because the government wants to have a sum of $16 million voted, not only to give a railway to the Gaspe peninsula but to develop its mining resources.
I have already quoted the letter from Mr. Westmore, manager of the St. Lawrence Corporation Limited of Three Rivers, in which he said he was interested in negotiating with three saw mills in the Gaspe peninsula, because his company was experiencing difficulties in obtaining wood waste products and he thought the construction of that railway line would enable them to get them more easily.
And there, Mr. Chairman, it is not a question of only 25,000 tons, as suggested by the hon. member for Port Arthur, but a much larger quantity. As a matter of fact, when we say 35,000 tons, the hon. member says it is 20,000 tons, and when we say 25,000 tons, he says 10,000.
Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that the production of wood waste could be doubled or even tripled.
Mr. Chairman, there is always talk in the nouse of considerable development, for

example in the Yukon or other regions of Canada. On many occasions, in this chamber, it has been said that a railroad was essential to the development of a region, and that such a service should come before and not after the development. If the development of our country had to wait until railway lines were built, very few industries would come to invest millions of dollars to develop our plants.
Mr. Chairman, I could make further observations, but I think I have answered some of the objections raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur. On another occasion, I would like to give more explanations.
Besides, we are not the first to recognize the need for a railway line in that region, because in 1881-that is going back a long time-the newspaper La Minerve said:
The Gaspe peninsula is a separate section of French Canada, as are the Magdalen islands or even old Acadia (which became part of Canada in 1867). It is little known in the province of Quebec itself. In the olden days, that area had its own government and had little to do with those of Quebec, Three Rivers and Montreal, which were a compact and homogeneous group. Nowadays, relations between them have become more frequent, without, however, taking on the intimate and entirely uniform nature which is characteristic of relations between other districts on the St. Lawrence.
We still look upon Gaspe and its people as some sort of distant colony, as brothers who are separated from us, in the same way as the Acadians. The situation is, first of all, due to the remoteness of Gaspe which is hundreds of miles away from Quebec city-and to the lack of communications in some parts of the peninsula,
The Gulf steamers and the Intercolonial have brought the Gaspe peninsula nearer to Canada and also to the rest of the continent. But the seaway is of little help and the railway is still far away from the real Gaspe district. People in the central areas, who went to settle those faraway places and dedicate themselves to their development-like Dr. Fortin and Dr. Robitaille- did even more to inform the people of Gaspe about us and to tell us about them.
It would be in the best interests of the Gaspe people to end their isolation. They could only benefit from such a move, particularly if it resulted in giving them a taste for farming and, moreover, enabling them to take advantage of our fisheries-
Well, Mr. Chairman, that reminds me of what a good physician in my riding said, the other day, when I was spending a short time in my district. This is what he said: "There is a lot of talk about separatism in the province of Quebec. Now, we, in Gaspe, have been separated for three quarters of a century."
He certainly was right. I am sure that all hon. members will approve the bill and rejoice with me, five years hence, that they voted for it.

Mr. Chairman, I think if anything could confirm one's suspicions about this particular action of the government it has been the immoderate and I think unfortunate attack by the parliamentary secretary upon the hon. member for Port Arthur. Throughout this debate that particular member has carried on an extremely conservative-with a small "c"-assessment based on completely economic lines. I think to impute hatred, even lack of interest, on the part of any hon. member of this house, in this national parliament of the people, no matter from what group or whatever province in any other part of the country, is extremely improper and unfortunate.
The hon. member for Port Arthur has been trying to find out what are the economic possibilities. The parliamentary secretary said there were great economic possibilities. Where are they? I am sure that every member of this committee, perhaps over the lunch hour, will sit and read this evidence given before the standing committee on railways, canals, and telegraph lines. If, afterwards, he can come to the same conclusion as the previous speaker I shall be very much surprised. I invite hon. members to do just that, to read this evidence and secure any feeling of confidence that this line would either be of any great benefit to the area or constitute a paying proposition or an economic reality.
The previous speaker misses the point. It is not that this group has no sympathy with the people in this area. It is not that at all. We simply state that one cannot solve all the social, economic and political problems of an area simply by building a railway. You can only spend money once, and $16 million is a great deal of money. The same sum put into a Gaspe development fund, which might encourage people to come into that area, might very well prove of far greater use than this line which could be an economic embarrassment to the community 10 or 20 years from now. As I say, we are interested in the development of this area, but we believe there are more realistic, more economic ways of dealing with this question than by putting down two lines of steel.

speechtext:
It was not the hon. member who brought up the subject of elections at all; it was the parliamentary secretary who, speaking from his seat, interjected this matter into the debate while the speech was going on. As I was saying, we are interested in the development of this area, but we believe this development can be accomplished in better ways than the one now suggested. We have just had the benefit of a report by a royal commission. So far that report has not been acted on by this government. I am not blaming the government; I am not suggesting there has been undue delay. I am simply stating that nothing has been done in connection with this report, and that this is a time for reassessment; it is not a time for building lines and for undermining the proposals in this report, which will have to be acted upon by the government when it comes to deal with the recommendations.
My hon. friend from Port Arthur has already drawn attention to this aspect of the question, so I shall not refer to this report at any length. However, I remind the committee that it is not only the hon. members of this house who have studied this report; its recommendations have left an impression across the whole country. I could draw the attention of the committee to an article by Walter Gray in the Globe and Mail of February 16 under the heading "Railways Looking for Cut-back Discover Friends in Commission". I should not take up time by reading from this article, but I would point out that these are the views which are held across this country. I wonder how hon. members in every part of this chamber are going to explain the building of this railway to their constituents on the basis of the economic prospects, or rather the lack of economic prospects revealed in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, at a time when the various railway companies in Canada are cutting back their services.
I come from a constituency which is off the main lines of the major railways in Canada. We have experienced a certain amount of cutback of services. An attempt has been made to slow down this cutting back, and naturally so because various economic groups in the

Canadian National Railways community are concerned about it, but on the whole there has been an intelligent understanding of the realities of our national transportation problems today; it is realized in the community that certain services are no longer feasible or economic.
I realize that these circumstances do not represent a complete comparison with development lines such as we are discussing here. I am simply saying that people across this country are ready and willing to accept a reasonable assessment of national rail transportation. They realize that we are in a new age and that other means of transportation may have to take the place of railways. They realize there might have to be a redevelopment of our old concepts of railway economics in certain areas. The hon. member for Port Arthur has told us there are lines in his constituency which are rusting away right now because services have been cut off completely. How can hon. members in any part of this chamber go to their constituents and explain why we should spend $16 million on a railway when there is no real assurance that it will help the economy of the area? If there were any agreements with mining companies or pulp and paper companies I think there would a good case to argue, but I do not think such a basis can be found in the transcript of the evidence which has been placed before this committee.
I wonder how hon. members in the Liberal party can support this line. Last fall they showed an apparent concern-no, I will say it was a real concern-about the Pine Point railway. The feeling on the part of this party was that the Pine Point railway was economically unrealistic. I ask hon. members in the Liberal party to compare the economic possibilities of the Pine Point railway with those of this railway. I think they will find that the disadvantage will lie on the side of the railway we are discussing at the present time, and I wonder how they will react to this problem when it comes to putting their opinions on record.
I do not intend to take up the time of the committee any longer. I simply ask hon. members to take a slow, reasonable look at this proposed railway and to read the evidence on the subject. I am sure the answer will be obvious.

Mr. Chairman, I have been sitting in this house for the past four years, and I wonder why the hon. members for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) and Peterborough (Mr. Pitman) are making such a fuss today.

I shall immediately take up the comparison made by the hon. member for Peterborough between the matter of the Pine Point railway and the bill on the Gaspe railway which is now before the house.
I do think the attitude taken by the members of the new party somewhat odd, and I would like to know whether, if the railway were built in some part of the province, or of the constituency of the member for Peterborough or Port Arthur, we would witness as much opposition and hear so many questions asked as to the ability of the railway to pay its own way by the people who are advocating the socialization of public services. How can these gentlemen reconcile their doctrine with the statements they made today? How can they reconcile the doctrine which they preach in public, through their leaders, not only their federal leader, but the leader of the party in the province of Quebec, Mr. Chartrand, among others, to the effect that public services must primarily serve the people without regard to the economy of those services, how can they reconcile this doctrine with the arguments which they have put forward against the bill in this house today? How can they, on the one hand, preach socialization for our provinces, and, on the other hand, get up in this house and say: "Look at what has been said before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and you will see that this railway will not be economically feasible."
One of these two alternatives must be right, Mr. Chairman: the railway will be economically feasible or it will not. If it is-and the member for Gaspe so contends-we have no reason to refuse to approve its construction. If, by chance it is not, it would be wrong to deny this area of the province of Quebec the development it hopes for.
Economists and people familiar with the subject have stated repeatedly that the province of Quebec has not received its fair share in the way of railways. There have been improvements recently, and here is one granted this year by the present government. Are we going to deny Gaspe its railway and access to the development it desires under the pretext that it will not be economically feasible, which is but an assumption? If my memory serves me right, the member for Gaspe noted before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines that the truckers associations of the area were not able to offer the required services and that a railway was necessary. The member for Gaspe brought evidence to

the effect that the producers and the manufacturers want this line because they do not have adequate services. This evidence was not denied before the committee.
If the member for Port Arthur has evidence to the effect that what the member for Gaspe stated before the committee on railways is not correct, let him bring it forward and we will then be able to discuss it. I wonder how these people who have voted in favour of the principle of the bill, on the motion for second reading, can now contradict themselves?
I ask them to be sincere and honest once and for all, to stop pretending in their conventions that they recognize the needs of the province of Quebec as much as those of other provinces, that they recognize national equality of the French Canadians of Quebec, while getting up in this house trying to convince the government to refuse an economic advantage to this important area of the province of Quebec. I am asking them to be honest once and for all, to take a definite stand. If they consider this railway as uneconomic, they should give up their theory that railways should first of all serve the public, the areas which need them, without regard to profits, without regard to surplus or deficit. They should take a definite stand and vote for or against this railroad building project. In this way we will be able to assess their sincerity and later on we will let the people judge for themselves.
The hon. member for Gaspe did not bring up the question of an election, but the hon. member for Peterborough did.
If the members of the new party are so courageous, if the members of the new deceased party are so courageous, let them go to the country and account for their actions in the next election.
But before that, let them vote for or against this measure on third reading. I invite the hon. members for Peterborough and Port Arthur to do so. Just vote against it and then we shall see if you are sincere.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall not tell my hon. friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm that I am leaving right away for Montreal, to meet the railway authorities for the very purpose he just mentioned, but I thank him very much for having mentioned my name and I know that he did so out of friendship.
Just the same, I feel that this railway which is called by the whole population of the lower St. Lawrence "The Gaspe railway" will be a factor of prosperity and development for that area in years to come.
When this government decided to build a "development" railway in that area, it made a decision which the future will prove to be right, I am sure.
Besides, is it not my hon. friend from Port Arthur who mentioned the fact that the Mac-Pherson royal commission, at page 145, volume 2 of its report, suggested that when a railway is not self-sustaining the first year of operation, instead of having the railway companies bear the operation deficit incurred or the capital depreciation, the government should face its responsibilities and undertake to pay those deficits through appropriate grants, but that it should never place the burden on the railways.
Well, that is precisely what we are doing; besides, it has been recommended, not only by the MacPherson royal commission, but also by the Turgeon royal commission. In 1951, the Turgeon report recommended exactly the same thing, namely not to let the C.N.R. suffer any deficit or losses as a result of noneconomical operations in the first years.
Now, my hon. friend from Port Arthur referred to the information we supplied to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, to the effect that the railway would not be self-sustaining the first years.
We acknowledged that fact. We admit that the volume of assured traffic is comparatively small at present. But we believe it is a fair minimum.

Canadian National Railways
Those were the figures obtained through a study of the present situation of industry and trade in that area.
I actually went to the Gaspe peninsula where I met businessmen and industrialists. They all explained to me that the construction of this line with the resulting lower freight rates, will enable them to develop their industries or business and to increase their production.
As a matter of fact, that is the problem and that is why no one ever thought of setting up industries in the Gaspe peninsula.
Industries already established in the area were not interested in further development because shipment of their output to the market of central Canada would be too costly.
They had to pay part of their shipping costs to the C.N.R., part to the Canada and Gulf Terminal and further costs for trucking. They will now have more reasonable shipping costs and that is precisely what is needed in the Gaspe peninsula.
As far as possibilities are concerned, we merely have to take an unbiased look at the situation to realize that in view of the mineral output in that area until now, and of the large quantity of standing pulpwood and timber, reasonable shipping costs are a necessity.
Above all, I believe that the main reason why the government is willing to take over, for a few years to come, the deficits of this line, is that it is the human thing to do. The area has over 100,000 industrious people. All they want is a chance to prove that they have not lost those qualities for which they have long been noted.
A moment ago, my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Pitman) was saying that it was awful to realize that there were places in Canada where a railway had been built to develop a certain mine, and once the mine had been closed, the railway remained inoperative and was rusting away.
It is precisely the great difference that exists between the proposed railway and the others which, fairly often, are built by the Canadian National Railways. In the case of a mine, as at Mattagami for instance, the railway winds its way through the bush, where there is not a single soul living. Well, I suggest it would be criminal on the part of the railway company or of the government to build such a railway if we had no guarantee it would be self-supporting. I think it is absolutely essential for the government and for railway


companies to have a clear and definite guarantee that those railways will be selfsupporting.
But the case of the Gaspe peninsula is quite different. We have there an area which has been developed for four hundred years. People have lived there for a few centuries. We find villages and a fully established community; all sorts of small industries are to be found there that did not have the opportunity of developing as they should have. Just the same, everything is there at present; there is a potential. Furthermore, there is an interesting potential in natural resources. Well, this is a challenge for us. Are we going to invest the taxpayers' money in a place like that?
In introducing this measure, I believe the government has made a courageous gesture, a gesture that the future will prove reasonable, a gesture which will substantially contribute to the development of one of the most picturesque and interesting areas in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who is most concerned with this railway has made some points on which I think I should try to touch. First of all, he said that I had made no mention of the lumber potential. I think I indicated in my previous speech that at the present time this was the one real source of traffic, but my point was that there was an alternative route into the Montreal market for much of the year by water, and that this means of shipping is usually and normally considered much cheaper than shipping by rail.

There are a couple of other points in relation to the potential of this line that I think need to be looked at. As found on page 38 of the evidence taken before the committee, the minister was asked at the bottom of the page about the potential of the region, and with reference to the north shore area across the St. Lawrence he said:
They are now in process of building a highway to Seven Islands. Most of the population that works on the north shore comes from the south shore. There is only one farm on the north shore; whereas the south shore is a farming community, and there was no connection between the two shores. This present government has instituted a ferry service between Rimouski and Baie Comeau. This service has been operating for a period of two months and is a tremendous success. Its success has been far beyond all expectations.
Then he went on to say:
Last week we authorized the building of a new ship, new harbour facilities and a new service between St. Simeon and Riviere du Loup; we are building a new wharf at Matane, and we have approved the establishment of a new "roll on, roll off'' service between Matane and Godbout. This new branch line will help to assist the ferry service between Ste. Anne des Monts and Seven Islands. Within a very few years I think you will have a completely different picture of the economic situation of the lower St. Lawrence.
It seems to me that these are very reasonable proposals. Anyone who has looked at the economic indicators knows that the north shore of the St. Lawrence has had a phenomenal development, and it is quite understandable that it has been a magnet in drawing people from the south shore. It is quite understandable that the farmers on the south shore, where this railway is going to be built, are looking forward to feeding the growing population on the north shore. It is also good to know that marine services and so on are being set up to enable this to be done.
But here again my point is that all of us know enough about rail services to realize that where you have a water haul, as in this case, rail service in terms of moving these farm goods to the ferry and then across to the north shore is just not feasible in economic terms. The railway cannot really fulfil a function in carrying perishables, such as most farm products are, for a distance of say 50 miles, to be transported thence across the St. Lawrence by ferry. I think the minister and his economic adviser will admit that this is an area where trucking is much more likely and almost certain to play the real role. So it seems to me that in the provision of farm products for the north shore region the railway in common sense really cannot fit into the picture.
In so far as the question of mineral production is concerned, the royal commission
Canadian National Railways emphasizes that we must build railway lines to exploit large volume tonnage where there is any kind of considerable haul because this is far and away the cheapest means of transport. But the point I think the minister has to acknowledge is that every railway today is out to get some kind of iron-clad agreement or guarantee within the general situation of the mining industry. I pointed out that this is the situation at the present time at Steep Rock.
I suggest to the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville that I have complained before in the house about a branch line that was built in my area, a completely uneconomic one, that went into Manitouwadge a few years ago, which was just straight wastefulness. I can tell him that north of Nakina on the Canadian National Railways we have a large ore body on which over $10 million has been spent in development, and I would not vote for a measure to put a branch line in there unless there was some kind of contract with Anaconda, which is doing the development. Steep Rock Iron Mines has a very large iron ore prospect in the area north of Sioux Lookout near lake St. Joseph. I think it would be folly for this government or the Canadian National to put a branch line in there, no matter what the mining promoter might want, until the mining promoter was prepared to give some kind of guaranteed tonnage over some period of time.
On page 33 of the committee evidence the minister is reported as saying:
-we have a letter from Mr. Beauchemln stating that the moment the railway is built he will go ahead with the development of the East Sullivan Mines deposit in that precise area. He has always shown a tremendous interest in a railway in that area, and he has always considered the construction of this line as one of the main conditions for the development or exploitation of those deposits.
Fine, but where is the contract? Where is the undertaking? All you have is a letter expressing a pious wish. We can only assume it is a pious wish if the Canadian National Railway demands contracts from mining promoters in other parts of the country and does not get one here. Why can you not get one here? This seems to me to be the question that should be answered. If these ore bodies are so good, and if the only thing impeding ore development is the question of rail facilities, let us get a contract and go ahead. Let us put the rail line right into the mine and not bother just going to Ste. Anne des Monts. It seems to me this is the reasonable thing to do. All over Canada we have

Canadian National Railways ore bodies proven up, but there are usually economic considerations that determine whether or not we should proceed with development. If these particular projects were at a stage of development where the tonnage was known and they had some idea of markets, then it would seem to me that they would be prepared to offer at least a tentative agrement. However, you have not got that.
There is another point I should like to make. I gather from a quick look at the geology of the area that most of the ore bodies that exist are not in the field of iron ore where you get the largest bulk shipments, but are in the field of base metals. It is very rarely that base metal ore is shipped for long distances because of the various weight factors. The ore is almost always treated and reduced to concentrate form on the property itself. This would not mean that there would not be a large tonnage of concentrates shipped, but nothing in the nature of the huge production that moves out of an iron range, something in the nature of millions of tons a year. I submit that this being the case, why justify a line like this on the basis of mineral development if you cannot get something concrete from the developer?
The hon. member for Gaspe made a point that this was nothing but, I think he said, a certain hatred in my heart toward the people of Quebec. I wanted to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that I have been talking to French Canadians in Quebec who are opposed to this line. I wanted to put their views on the record. I did not find I could not deal with them. I have here a copy of a letter sent to the hon. member for Gaspe signed by Romeo Blouin, secretary general, Quebec trucking association.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE BETWEEN MATANE AND STE. ANNE DES MONTS, QUE.
speechtext:
Before the luncheon adjournment I put on the record a letter sent by the Quebec trucking association to the hon. member for Gaspe. This letter was occasioned by a press report referring to the evidence that the hon. member for Gaspe gave before the committee, in relation to objections from the trucking organization.
The motion that is referred to by the secretary of the Quebec trucking association is motion No. 28, and I should like to read it as it has been forwarded to me by the association in translation form. It is entitled "Why a railroad in the Gaspesia region," and reads as follows:
In the speech from the throne, upon the opening of the parliament in Ottawa, the federal government has announced the construction of a railroad, out of the public funds, at the cost of $16 million, in the Gaspesia peninsula, from Matane to Ste. Anne des Monts, namely a distance of about bO miles.
Whereas the MacPheirson royal commission of inquiry on transportation has recommended the abandonment by the railways of non-profitable
services;
Whereas three trucking! companies, bus lines, local truckers and taxi companies have invested moneys and are already at the disposal of the public in that region of the province of Quebec, to transport goods or passengers;
Whereas these transport enterprises operate their services without public subsidies;

It is moved to ask the federal government to make a survey in that region to find out if the trucking firms, bus and taxi lines meet the public needs. If those services are satisfactory and that the survey recommends that to help the Gaspesia region, there should be a reduction of rates, subsidies be granted to the existing enterprises rather than investing $16 million in an enterprise which will never be profitable and would constantly be a burden upon the taxpayers.
Whatever other appeal that argument may-have I think it certainly makes the point that there is a strong body of opinion in the province of Quebec which has no relationship to me, and I would say no particular interest in me, but which is objecting to this railroad. I would ask the hon. member for Gaspe to remember that, when he makes the charge that I am speaking only out of some kind of hatred in my heart.
I would underline again that I represent the fourth largest constituency in Canada. It has more miles of railroad track in it than any other constituency in Canada. At its broadest point there are 365 miles of transcontinental railway. Two transcontinental railways run through it and in addition there are a number of branch lines, although I can truly say that some of those branch lines are practically rusting at the present time.
Now it seems to me that this is enough reason to be critical of this line even if one has not the national picture at heart and if one is not interested in the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation.
I do appreciate the rebuttal argument, if one could call it that, made by the Minister of Transport. He seems to suggest that there is no possibility of getting industries interested in the Gaspesia area until there is rail transportation provided there. However I can tell him that there are many parts of the country which do have rail transportation and they do not seem to be able to get industries interested in them. There are places in southern Ontario-I am thinking of communities such as Barrie which has had a great development in industry of the most desirable kind, secondary industry, clustered around that town-where the railway services have been restricted and restrained. In other words the indication is that the incentives which bring secondary manufacturers into an area usually depend less upon transportation than upon access or relationship to markets.
The argument is made that industries cannot get to markets from the Gaspesia region because of the lack of a railroad but my point is that, on the grounds of distance from any place there to the large cities such as Quebec and Montreal, the difference between rail transportation and truck transportation is in many cases nil unless you have a large volume of tonnage that can be looked upon in some
26207-1-105
Canadian National Railways way as capital that is going to develop. This large volume of tonnage can only come from products of the forests and mines, and here we have nothing but very nebulous promises.
The hon. member for Chambly-Rouville brought up a good debating point. He made the suggestion that the particular party I am associated with has a certain argument that it is presenting to Quebec at the moment and he wondered whether my approach was not a contradiction of it in that, in a sense, it seemed to be an anti-socialist argument. I do not know what conception one has of what a socialist is in Canada but I would hope that whether one is a socialist, a capitalist, a Liberal, a Conservative or a Social Crediter, as a member of parliament no matter what one's background might be he would want to see enterprises approved by parliament that had a good future and that really dovetailed into some kind of an operational plan.
I return again to the evidence. The C.N.R. representative who appeared before our committee was not pressed deeply on any question but there is no indication in this evidence that the C.N.R. has even surveyed the situation for potential in the particular region. As a matter of fact there is no indication of what kind of rates may be struck. It was suggested that the ordinary rates would apply; that is, the railway has not even given this the consideration of what kind of incentives it can bring.
I had the impression-perhaps the minister can contradict this-that the C.N.R. officials who will be constructing this line and running it have not had any relationship with this great copper property at Murdochville or this potential East Sullivan property of Mr. Beauchemin. This I can only look upon as inadequate planning. I do not use the word "planning" in a nagging sense, but surely for an expenditure of this scale there should be some kind of projection by the agent who is going to have the responsibility.
It comes down to this. Can this railway line carry passengers effectively? The answer is no. There is hardly a railway line anywhere in North America today, except in the most concentrated populated areas, that is carrying passengers effectively to make any money. What else can it carry, then, other than freight? Is this the kind of region that is going to have a great deal of piggyback services or concentrated market services where there is a fairly large volume of high rated traffic going to be generated? Not at all. And it is already served by the St. Lawrence waterway, in my opinion the greatest waterway in the world.

Canadian National Railways
I understand that the Gaspe region is well served by air transportation, or at least comparatively well served. The trucking association claims that there is a good trucking set up in there at the present time and that there is a competitive trucking set up there. I am not suggesting that we should accept their argument in toto, but we have no indication that the C.N.R. has looked into this aspect of it. We were told at the committee that the C.N.R. had no plans for using its trucking operations to dovetail into this extension of the branch line; in other words, they have not even gone that far to build up a conception of service around this line. It is for all these reasons that we have grave doubts about the line.
There is one other point that I think needs to be underlined, and that is the position of the provincial government in this whole matter. I admire this government for its efforts in the field of the roads to resources program, its attempt to work out in forestry and other fields a co-operative program that brings federal and provincial initiative together for development projects. I cannot find any indications in the record that the roads to resources program has been touched upon at all in this particular region; that there have been any demands or requests for it. I must admit that I have only looked at the records that have been provided me about the roads to resources program. Maybe there has been something, but I have not been able to find it. But we have from the minister himself an indication that he has not been in touch with the provincial authorities on this matter, and I would just like to note that on the record. I asked the minister this question:
In Ontario much of the development in railway-extension is taking place under provincial auspices. What approach did you make to the government of the province here in order to work out some kind of arrangement under which they would bear part of the cost?
I went on to ask another question:
What approach did you make to the province to get assistance or support?

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE BETWEEN MATANE AND STE. ANNE DES MONTS, QUE.
speechtext:
We did not make any.
I went on:
Could you tell me why you did not? The reason I ask is that before the royal commission on transportation a Quebec minister gave evidence in which he indicated that the province of Quebec was ready to build a railway line if necessary to help development.
I did not mean for this particular area; I meant generally, of course. My question went on:
Since that time Mr. Levesque has also indicated that the Quebec government would not hesitate,


in order to develop the province, to build railway lines. With statements of that kind on the record and with a project which in the short run you say is uneconomic, why was the province not drawn in for assistance?
Here is the minister's answer:
We feel that this project should have been built a long time ago, and that it is a federal responsibility. The federal government is convinced that the long term benefits from this railway will prove we acted wisely when we built the railway.
Here you have a situation where a provincial minister appearing before a royal commission on transportation sets out a bunch of potential branch lines for the province. As a matter of fact the minister who did it is a brother of the hon. member from Chambly-Rouville. I thought the presentation he made before the royal commission was an excellent one; it put the case for development railways in Quebec as I read it, and I certainly understood that the Quebec government was ready to give the lead and if necessary to take the lead in development railways.
Given that situation, plus the statements of Mr. Levesque, why were not the provincial governments approached? Here is the government that is in charge of mineral resources; here is the government that is in charge of forest resources-and the minister himself says these are basic to the development-and yet they did not bother to approach that government to see whether this was the line they wanted or whether it would dovetail in any way. Could the minister indicate that the provincial government is going to support this development with any concrete plans? I do not get that impression from the evidence, and I think the minister should tell us. Until he tells us I can only assume that no liaison has been established at all with the provincial government in connection with this matter. The minister seems to rest his case upon this, that it should have been built a long time ago and that it is a federal responsibility.
Surely in view of the royal commission we are not building railways today to make up for something that was not done some years ago; surely we are building them because they are going to serve an economic need. Given this kind of a situation, I wonder how the government can proceed with this kind of an expenditure that I know on the face of it is attractive, but without any liaison or project in unison with the provincial government.
This government has, I think-I was going to say made great play, but that might suggest something nasty-certainly given the impression that it is anxious at all times to work co-operatively with the provinces, and this is an attempt to develop a region of a

province through its natural resources. Yet, Mr. Chairman, the minister has not bothered to talk to the province concerned about it at all. I can only express surprise and certain regret about that.
There is one other point. The hon. member for Gaspe pointed out that this would create work in the Gaspe region. Of course it will: building a line does. But I should like to refer him to the words that were given to us by the Minister of Public Works on this very question as to whether public projects could be any substantial answer to the unemployment situation. I think the minister will remember these words. I have not them here, but I think I can remember the gist of them fairly well. He said that the unemployment problem could not be met in the long run by building public projects. It seems to me that is a point of view of the government that would gainsay the argument that this is or could be primarily a project to meet the unemployment situation.
Surely, there are more effective ways of spending money in that area. At the present time the area seems to be served by highways and by water for approximately eight months of the year. It seems to have some air facilities. It has neither rail nor pipe line facilities. I would reiterate that today this is not considered to be a major lack in most parts of the North American continent unless the transportation demand or need is for large volume traffic usually related to products of the forest or of the mine. In this particular case I submit we really have not had the evidence that this is the potential.
When I am moving around the country I often hear from people about the cadre of experts and economic wizards which the federal government seems to be building up here in Ottawa. People say the civil service is expanding at a fantastic rate-that the government is plucking bright people from the universities and sticking them in, with the result that we are getting a top heavy bureaucracy that is likely to plan far too much of our lives and activities. All I do in this regard is to refer these people to the branch line proposed between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts, because this seems to me a case where these economic experts have made practically no contribution at all and where the investigations which have been conducted turn out, at the most, to be tentative and sketchy.

I remember the promises those politicians used to make in my constituency, the riding of Rimouski, when as a young student I was getting interested in the material problems of the district.

Realizing that transportation facilities are the basis and, in a way, the lifeblood of our district's economy, the Minister of Transport has kindly taken the necessary action in that respect and has introduced the bill under consideration to put an end to the procrastination favoured by the Liberals.
Moreover, this is but one item in the general program which is being carried out in my area. I should like to mention another concrete measure from which taxpayers in my constituency are already benefiting. Father Point and Baie Comeau are now connected by means of a year-round ferry service.
With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to an interruption recently made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), during the debate on the resolution. The hon. gentleman, in a desperate attempt to save his party's chances, undertook to repeat the suggestions contained in a report prepared by the distinguished professor, Mr. Camu, on "Transportation problems in the lower St. Lawrence region''. One of Mr. Camu's suggestions was the establishment of three ferry services, including one between

Mr. Chairman, there was a point raised by the hon. member on which I want to touch. I should like to tell him that my own particular imagination in relation to this rail line would have been much more attracted and I would have conceived it as much more imaginative if the rail line was going to go all the way through say to Murdochville or all the way round the Gaspe coast. I should like to point out to him that it is only an extension of a line that exists at the present time. There is no indication from the minister that it is to be anything more than that.
The other point he made, and it was made by other members, is that Gaspe has been asking for this line for 50 years. Well, 50 years ago was the railway age; that was when railways were important for transporting goods. But the experience in recent years has been different, otherwise we would not have truckers appearing all over the place giving evidence; we would not have presidential commissions or the royal commission on transportation going into this whole matter. All these things mean there are great problems in connection with the over-expansion of railways.
I want to put on the record a point Mr. Donald Gordon of Canadian National Railways made a few years ago in relation to the expansion of rail lines, branch lines, so far as the Canadian National Railway is concerned. I am quoting from page 227 of the evidence of the 1955 committee on railways and shipping. At the time, Mr. Gordon was being queried by the present member for
Canadian National Railways Notre Dame de Grace and the present member for Greenwood. The present member for Greenwood said:
What do the words "traffic guarantee" mean?
The question was asked in relation to the development of branch lines by Canadian National. Mr. Gordon's reply was as follows:
It is a formula which we have devised which may apply in different ways. For example, to give you one example take the building of our line from Terrace to Kitimat, B.C. There we are servicing one industry. At the time that industry was proposed we said to the Aluminum Company: "We will build a line if you can satisfy us that traffic will be forthcoming" and they said: "Of course it will be forthcoming". We said: "Well, how do we know your plans are going to work out? We are not prepared to build the line and find nothing there. If you will undertake with us to provide a specified amount of traffic and undertake to reimburse us if you don't provide it, we will build the line."
Now, if the traffic materializes it costs them nothing.
He is referring there to the Kitimat organization.
If the traffic does not materialize then they put us in the position as if the traffic had materialized. That is a simple form of traffic guarantee, but when we get into a line of this kind it becomes more complicated.
He is referring here to the line between Chibougamau, St. Felicien and Beattyville. Mr. Gordon goes on:
I am not too sure we can work it out. because a great number of shippers may be involved, but if we can get enough traffic guaranteed from individual shippers of a kind which we can depend on, assuring us of traffic, then we would be willing to build the line.
Now, that does apply to the Beattyville-Chibou-gamau branch that we are building now. We have received traffic guarantees from the interested shippers which will justify us in building the line. Incidentally of course, like all these things, there are many facets to the agreement, and we credit the line with the freight that may materialize whether it is from those shippers or not.
Now that, it seems to me, is a very clear and succinct outline of how Canadian National Railways approaches the building of branch lines. It is quite apparent that Canadian National would not touch this particular branch line as part of its normal program. They have to go ahead because the minister has accepted responsibility and the government is putting up the money. The government is going to look after the deficits or profit whatever the case may be. The Canadian National is merely the agent, and as the agent of the government the Canadian National has to do what it is told. There is no quarrel about this at all. We did not get any indication, Mr. Chairman, from the Canadian National witnesses who appeared before the committee that the Canadian National had even looked into the construction of this

Canadian National Railways line very deeply. Now, what kind of railway building scheme is it when the government agency has not looked into it?
In 1955 Mr. Gordon told, and he has repeated it almost every year in one form or another before every committee, how careful the Canadian National is not to get itself into some kind of scheme that is not going to have some future in it. Hon. members of this house know that I am not a great admirer of the president of Canadian National Railways. This may be an understatement. Certainly, however, I have the impression he will build a branch line when he thinks there are any prospects at all for business. He will send his men in, they will work out surveys and make agreements. They will ask shippers. They will do all these things and yet, in so far as this line is concerned, I should like to point out again Canadian National does not seem to have done these things. Surely, we have no better underline-ment of the economic weaknesses of this line.
In order to conclude my remarks at this stage of the bill, I should like to reiterate that I feel it is a very bad day for the parliament of Canada when a member gets up to express views about something that fits into the national transportation picture-at least the minister indicated it fitted into the national transportation picture-and he is told by other members of the house, in effect, he should really mind his own business; that this is outside of his province. He should sit and, I suppose, listen to the people who come from that particular area. This is a point of view that I cannot do any more than regret.
But I should like to make it very clear that if anyone wants to criticize railway developments in northwestern Ontario or in Port Arthur-I have a hunch we will be getting a branch line or two in the next few years-I would say they would be more than welcome. I do not see how you can look at the railway transportation picture in this country without being worried about the scale of development. Only in the last few weeks, I have been involved in negotiations relating to union contracts. I have just finished reading the presidential report in the United States, which is going to have ramifications in the Canadian situation. We are going to get the Canadian National annual report very shortly, and it is going to show another substantial deficit. We are going to have deficits on both private and public air lines, in the transcontinental sense.
There is nothing in our transportation picture where railways are concerned, that leads us to be optimistic about their capacity to meet the immediate challenge unless we 
open up and change our whole attitude towards transportation. Although I may disagree, and I have known all kinds of other people much more expert than I am who disagree, with some of the recommendations in the report of the royal commission on transportation, I fail to see how the government can go ahead with this particular project with so little research and so little planning. It seems to me to reveal quite a lot of the recommendations in this volume upon which I think the government will be acting very early.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to answer briefly a few of the questions that have been asked. I want to say right now that I am not going to repeat for the fifteenth time the same arguments and answer the same questions that were answered both here in the house at the time of the resolution and in detail in the committee.
The hon. member for Port Arthur and the hon. member for Timmins tried to make a great big case and cause great excitement over the fact that we have not consulted the province of Quebec. This has not been done in 25 years by any government building railroads in Canada. The provinces have never been consulted. They do not want to be consulted, because they tell us "Look, railways are your baby. Don't try to get any money out of us to build railways; we are
[Mr. Martin (Timmins) .1

not interested". So it is absolutely utopian to think that the province of Quebec will give us money to build railroads. There are two provincial railways in Canada, and they do not come to us for money with which to build railroads. They would laugh at us if we went to them and asked for money to build railroads. This is exactly what will happen in the province of Quebec. This has never been done.
The hon. member for Timmins, following the hon. member for Port Arthur, raised the matter that no proper study has been made of the project, that we did not have any reports, and so on. The Canadian National Railways has made many studies of this situation; they have made reports to the Department of Transport and to myself. In 1957 they made a very extensive study and came to the conclusion that it was not in the interests of Canadian National Railways to build a line themselves, but they made a very detailed report to the department. It was on these reports and on other studies made by economists of the department and private individuals-quite independent economists- and also taking into account the great contribution of the chambers of commerce and different organizations in the area, that we reached this decision. Since I have been Minister of Transport it has always fascinated me to see the great effort that is being made in this part of the province of Quebec by the people helping themselves before coming to the government to try to obtain handouts. In the lower St. Lawrence the chambers of commerce got together; they set up study groups and hired economists and engineers to make special surveys. They have paid for that, and these reports have been extremely helpful to the experts of my department. All these various reports and factors were considered by the government in reaching the decision to go ahead with this railway.
As far as the MacPherson report is concerned, there is nothing in that report which says the government should stop building development railways. The MacPherson report made a great difference between national policy and a national transportation policy. The railway being considered by the committee at the present time is a development railway, and as such it is a matter of national policy and should be the responsibility of the government. The government did not saddle the Canadian National Railway with the expenses of this railway; this is absolutely in line with the MacPherson royal commission report and with the philosophy of that report. Therefore I do not think we have to worry, because it is not going against the recommendations of the MacPherson royal commission report.

Of course, we are all anxious to see this railway line pay, and it will pay. It is a matter of when it will start to pay after the amortization of the capital. Personally I am very confident that it will come sooner than we think, because we have examples in this area of Canada that the people are hard working and are determined to see their natural resources exploited and developed so they can carry on living in the area and building up a future for their children.

speechtext:
