He said: The purpose of this bill is to set a limit of 1 per cent per month as the maximum interest rate which could be

charged by small loans companies on loans up to $1,000. The reason it is worded in this way is that the Small Loans Act at this time sets a smaller rate for loans in excess of $1,000. As long ago as 1955, Mr. Speaker, I had the honour to introduce in this house a bill which would limit the interest rates on small loans to 1 per cent per month. At that time there were very few facilities available to many people in the country who wished to obtain small loans for personal needs. The measure that I presented at that time received a good deal of support across this country. I had a great many communications at that time in support of that general proposition and I have had a great many since then.
In 1956 the government of the day brought in a government measure which was sent to the banking and commerce committee of this house and which went some distance toward reducing interest rates that could be charged by small loans companies.
Up until 1956 the maximum rate was 2 per cent per month on loans from zero to $500. Beyond that point there was no control. In 1956, the measure of that day set an interest limit of 2 per cent per month on loans from zero to $300; 1 per cent per month on loans of $300 to $1000; and one half of one per cent per month on loans from $1,000 to $1,500. This was an important step forward.
Those who spoke at that time on behalf of the small loans companies in this country said that the measure of that day would bring financial ruin to the small loans companies. They said it would mean that they would be going out of business, that they would be obliged to curtail their loans. This dire forecast has not been fulfilled. The small loans companies have continued to expand and to increase their business and their profits. However, the campaign, if I might call it that, which was started in this parliament in 1955 has been continued since then and, I would suggest, has received a more sympathetic hearing year after year.
The problem of high interest rates charged to ordinary borrowers has impressed itself on a larger and larger number of members of this house. The problem, of course, is not confined to small loans companies and loans from small loans companies only. The problem results in the tremendous or fantastic interest rates that are very often charged on second mortgages-these fantastic interest rates may go as high as 20 per cent or 25 per cent per year-and the fantastic rates that are often charged on instalment credit. In other words, the ordinary small borrower with a low income who had to borrow for personal purchases, for household purchases or in order to deal with family emergencies,

very often in the past has been a victim of the unscrupulous lender who has charged very high interest rates.
Some people have decided to attack this problem from various angles. When I first introduced this bill the then hon. member for Saskatoon, Mr. R. R. Knight, introduced another bill which, if it had been passed, would have made it necessary for small loans companies in their advertising to set forth the interest rate they would charge. An amplification of or an improvement on this idea was brought forward in the Senate last year by Senator Croll. There is before the other place at this time a bill which would provide that in any loans made by financial institutions the actual interest charged must be set forth in the contract. The hon. member for Rosthern this year in this chamber introduced a bill which is similar to the bill introduced in the other place.
These are two good bills. I hope the bill in the other place reaches a vote and I hope that it is passed. I hope the bill of the hon. member for Rosthern might reach a vote in this session and be passed. That is a hope I have, Mr. Speaker, but it is not much more than that. We all know what happens to private members' bills; and with the new arrangement-and I am not complaining about it; I think it is an improved arrangement-with a one hour debate, the chance of a bill coming to a vote, unless all of the parties wish it to do so, is indeed extremely remote. However, the fact that a member of this house and a member of the other place have decided this field was important enough to warrant their putting forward bills asking that the interest rate be set forth in contracts so that the borrower might readily understand the interest rates that must be paid is, in my opinion, a very good omen. I have had on the order paper another bill which would set a general interest ceiling across this country of one per cent per month. If such a measure were passed by this house, then of course this particular measure with its more detailed application would not be necessary.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the time has arrived once again when the whole problem of high interest rates charged by small loans companies, finance companies and moneylenders and including interest rates charged on second mortgages and on instalment credit, should be referred to the banking and commerce committee of the house. I believe that witnesses should be called, that evidence should be heard and that parliament itself should decide to deal with this very important problem in a more effective way than it has been dealt with in the past.
Small Loans Act
In recent years there have been some improvements in this general field of lending money to lower income earners and in lending money at lower interest rates. A very important institution in this country and one of growing importance is the credit union or the caisse populaire. The credit unions are serving the Canadian nation well in a very important way. The credit unions across this country are growing and are providing an excellent service. I have in my hand a publication which is entitled "Credit Unions in Canada, 1960" and which is published by the economics division, Canada Department of Agriculture. It shows that in 1960 there were 4,667 chartered credit unions in Canada with a membership of 2,544,300 and that the number has been growing at a very significant rate. In 1950, for example, there were 2,965 chartered credit unions with a membership at that time of just over one million, being 7.5 per cent of the population. By 1960 membership in the credit unions was 2,554,300, being 13.9 per cent of the Canadian population, and assets had increased from $312 million in 1950 to $1,299 million in 1960.
Credit unions provide credit to their membership at cost. They charge as a maximum rate 1 per cent per month, and they have been able to do a large and successful business. As a matter of fact, many credit unions are able to pay dividends both to persons who have invested money in the credit union and to the persons who are borrowing money from it.
The 1 per cent interest rate that I have suggested in this bill would not in any way affect the credit unions, and I think their success together with the success of the small loans companies with the new interest rates of 1956 suggest that if this bill were passed even the small loans companies would be able to continue in business and make a return.
There are a great many credit unions that charge much less than 1 per cent per month. In the province from which I come the credit unions very often charge rates of 6, 7 or 8 per cent per year depending on the type of loan. I belong to two or three credit unions.

speechtext: Do you need that many?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE MAXIMUM INTEREST RATE
speechtext: Oh, I find it is a little easier to borrow sometimes if you have more than one opportunity to do so.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE MAXIMUM INTEREST RATE
speechtext: Spread the risk.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE MAXIMUM INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
I try also to pay my accounts on time. One credit union to which I belong is the Assiniboia credit union which makes the boast of being the largest rural credit union in Canada with assets, I believe, of some $4J million. Their lending rate is 7 per

Small Loans Act
cent and loans are life insured so that if the borrower should die the loan is automatically paid up out of their life insurance fund and the estate of the deceased does not have to meet that obligation. In addition, this large and successful credit union in a town in rural Saskatchewan last year paid to the borrower a 10 per cent patronage dividend on the interest that he had paid. In other words, the net interest rate worked out to 6.3 per cent, and this for a life insured loan. I think this indicates an excellent type of lending institution from the standpoint of the small borrower in this particular community.
Credit unions have done and are doing a marvellous job in this country and I am sure that the role they play will be a greater one in the years ahead. I might say that in my experience the credit unions have received the support of the whole community in which they operate. Farmers, small business people, workers and professional people all find that it is to the general advantage of the community itself to have a place where local funds can be deposited, where they can be lent to borrowers who need those funds and where the funds generated in the community will bring about the greatest possible benefit to the community as a whole. So this is an alternative form of borrowing for many who in the past have had to go to small loans companies to get money.
Another alternative form is the chartered banks themselves which in recent years have gone into the small loans field in a very large and successful way and I am sure in a very welcome way. In 1957, for example, loans on the security of household property amounted to less than $8 million while in 1961 the total was $224 million. Other personal loans in 1957 amounted to $400 million while at the end of 1961 the total was over $800 million.
The banks have promoted the small loans field in recent years. Their branches in the cities and towns are being established in the suburban areas and the shopping centres where they are available to meet to a substantial degree the borrowing needs of citizens within the area. This is another method of attacking this very important problem. I am proud of the accomplishments of the past in reducing the cost of small loans to borrowers. I am very pleased with the growing use of credit unions and with the development of the personal loans divisions within the chartered banks.
There are further problems at this time with respect to high interest rates in the second mortgage field and on much instalment credit. This is a great problem. It is receiving more sympathetic consideration from members in all parts of the house. I should like to see

this measure passed. As an alternative I should like to see it sent to the banking and commerce committee so that a further study of the general problem might be made and such bills as those presented in the other place and that of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) in conjunction with this one might be studied to the end that the credit needs of ordinary Canadians might be supplied at the lowest possible interest rate.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE MAXIMUM INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-19 which is before us this afternoon proposes an amendment to the Small Loans Act. As has been set forth, the situation at the present time is that under the Small Loans Act a charge of 2 per cent per month may be levied on all loans or balances of loans under $300. Interest of 1 per cent per month may be charged on loans exceeding $300 and up to $1,000 and, in the third category, a charge of one half of one per cent per month on loans over $1,000. The bill would place a ceiling of 1 per cent per month on all loans up to $1,000 and then one half of one per cent on loans over $1,000.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I have noted considerable interest among members of the house in the matter of small loans financing and instalment buying in general. There are now some three bills on the order paper which are concerned with this matter, and I think one of the best is that introduced by the member for Rosthern, Bill No. C-6, which would require the cost of servicing these loans to be shown as a percentage of principal. I am sorry I was unable to be present in the house when this bill came up for debate but I had to be in my riding at the time. If I had been here I would have supported the member for Rosthern in what I believe to be a very worthy objective.
I have also noted a very wide interest throughout the country in this matter of consumer financing, and interest rates on small loans. I believe other members of the house have the same experience as I, that they are receiving many letters from day to day on this topic urging that some inquiry be made into the situation. Certainly the problem of consumer financing today, grown as it has to become a giant in the financial world in the nation, is one that concerns everyone.
Only a few years ago the chief lender in the nation was the bank, even for the purpose of a small loan. Now the situation is much more complicated with many borrowers going to small loan companies. Much credit is put out by acceptance corporations which underwrite quite a bit of the merchandising of the nation. I have felt that as this business has grown there has grown with it the need for some form of protection for the consumer of credit similar to the protection that is set

up for the consumers of general merchandise to protect people from fraudulent types of credit just as they are protected from fraudulent merchandising.
I remember not long ago trying a court case at home in which a man had signed an instalment contract in blank to purchase a car. Later, the car was repossessed and an action was brought against him to recover the balance owing on the vehicle after the car had been sold. He came into court to say that he had no idea at all that the finance charges would be as much as they were; that this was a different deal from the one to which he had agreed with the car dealer. The judge felt that the deal seemed to be pretty close to what the dealer represented it to be and he required the defendant in the case to stand by his contract, although he had signed it in blank. The buyer had put his signature on this instalment contract, it had been endorsed for value, and he was therefore, held liable for it. I merely state this to show how often people are deceived into signing documents of this type, and how lightly some enter upon a transaction which could be quite important. Many people who will shop widely for good prices on merchandise will slip very quickly into a proposition that requires them to pay a large amount for carrying charges on the products they buy.
As I have said, I see considerable interest in the country in this problem. Just the other day I had a note from a friend of mine who came originally from Cape Breton but who is now living in Ottawa and is interested in social work. He sent me a clipping from the Western Producer about the bill introduced by the hon. member for Rosthern and suggested I support that bill. In his letter which he attached to the clipping, he simply said, "Bob, is there any way a private member like yourself can help this proposal?" Well, I think that indicates two things: One is the amount of interest of a lot of people in this sort of thing and, second, how very few people realize how much impact the opinion of a private member in the house has upon the government in matters of this kind.
As hon. members are aware, we now have a royal commission on this subject which will be conducting hearings all across Canada in the months to come. I refer to the royal commission on banking and finance in Canada, the appointment of the members of which was announced by the Prime Minister on October 18. It is under the chairmanship of the distinguished Mr. Dana H. Porter, chief justice of Ontario. The other commissioners are, Mr. W. Thomas Brown, of Vancouver, British Columbia; Mr. James Douglas Gibson, of Toronto; Mr. Gordon L. Harrold of Calgary; Mr. Paul H. Leman, Montreal; Dr. W.
Small Loans Act
A. Mackintosh, Kingston; and Mr. John C. MacKeen, a well known businessman from my own province of Nova Scotia. All of these men have excellent qualifications for this work which is before them. The commission is now active; the secretariat has been set up and, as I said, hearings will commence across the nation very soon.
The terms of reference of the royal commission are very broad. They will be considering matters of the kind proposed in this bill today as well as matters of the type proposed in the bill introduced by the hon. member for Rosthern. I think this is an example of how quickly the government acts in matters of this kind, where private members have advocated measures which would deal with consumer financing and have suggested that an inquiry should be made. As hon. members will recall, when bills similar to this were before the house before, most members were inclined to be cautious about having such bills passed. However, many did suggest that an inquiry should be made into the whole field of consumer financing. As a result the government has launched this commission, and it surprises me how few people in the nation seem to know that the inquiry is going ahead. Indeed, the hon. member for Assiniboia suggested that a special committee should be set up to inquire into consumer financing and interest rates. I wonder if he realizes that these matters will be gone into by the royal commission?

speechtext: I have more faith in us than in a royal commission.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE MAXIMUM INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
I would say the best way to examine this question and make the detailed inquiry necessary would be by means of a royal commission. They have the staff, they have the facilities and the time to go into this matter very fully, to a much greater extent than we could here in a committee. However, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put on the record the statement of the Minister of Finance when he announced in the commons on June 20, 1961, that this royal commission would be set up later. Speaking of the terms of reference of the commission at that time, as reported on page 6648 of Hansard for June 20, 1961, he said:
Meanwhile, I say that the terms of reference will be broad, covering all aspects of money, banking, credit and finance. The financing of the Canadian economy will be one of the major areas of study. Such broad topics as the pattern and behaviour of interest rates, consumer credit and instalment financing, and the management of the public debt, will be included in the terms of reference. The commission will be asked to study existing financial institutions, such as the chartered banks, the Bank of Canada, and other institutions that perform banking and credit functions, and the various acts of parliament which govern their activities.

Small Loans Act
The commission will also be asked to consider ways and means of encouraging the development of savings institutions. It would be our intention that the report of the commission should be available well in advance of the decennial review of the Bank Act.
I put that on the record to show that this royal commission will be going into matters covered by this bill today. I would suggest to the house that this bill should not be passed until we have had an opportunity to see the report of the royal commission following their exhaustive inquiry.
I am very pleased to see this inquiry taking place. As I have stated on previous occasions in this house, this is a very complicated issue and one which needs to be examined, certainly one which should have a very careful and exhaustive examination before precipitate action is taken. It is very easy to say that 12 per cent should be enough interest for anyone to earn on a loan and indeed, of course, at first blush it is. However, there are many situations, as all hon. members are aware, in which high risk credit is required and this rate may not be high enough to make the loan attractive to the lender. Rates depend on many factors which are always fluctuating. I doubt very much if it would be in the interest of the nation to limit the rate of interest as this bill suggests, without first of all looking fully into all the aspects of the case. Of course, I am in accord with the general principle of the bill.
The rates that are charged at any given time in any sector of the economy will depend upon the money supply at the time, the demands for loans of the type in question and the risk which is involved, as well, of course, as the cost of administering the loan. Everyone will realize that 6 per cent on a $10,000 mortgage loan can be obtained with very much less administration cost than on the same $10,000 advanced in 100 small loans. The administration needed for each of these 100 loans could be even greater than on a mortgage loan of $10,000 which had real estate security behind it. It has been pointed out that credit unions get by with a rate of 1 per cent per month. It has been my experience, working closely with credit unions, that there are many types of loans which a credit union must decline because it wants to keep the interest rates down. They normally require the endorsement of someone having funds on deposit in the credit union, or some other type of endorsement that will more or less guarantee the loan. Many loan companies and instalment companies lend money only on the value of goods, and their security is not nearly as strong in the case of default as the endorsement of a guarantor.
[Mr. MacLellan.j
However there can be no question but that the whole subject of consumer financing is very important and has very widespread economic and social effects. Indeed one is often surprised at the lack of knowledge shown by many people as to what they actually pay for money and what interest costs on many of these instalment transactions. Some time ago I was reading a book which I know is familiar to many hon. members. It is entitled "The Organization Man" by William H. Whyte, Jr. The book deals generally with the development of the new white-collar group in the United States, the young executive people who are climbing the ladder in industry and business, and it surveyed generally the life of the new suburbia which has grown up in the last 20 years.
The book is very interesting, particularly chapter 24, where the author writes of the results of surveys made into the buying and saving habits of these young executives in the suburbs of the larger cities. I think it would be well to bear in mind that the people of whom he speaks are not uneducated people. Most of them have college education or are graduates of high schools. If anyone should understand the mysteries of instalment buying and the cost of credit, and should be able to apply that knowledge, surely these people would be the ones. But this is what Mr. Whyte says as a result of the surveys he has conducted in many of the big subdivisions in the United States. I am quoting from page 326:
For a future capitalist, the organization man displays a remarkable inability to manipulate capital. His handling of "debt consolidation" is a case in point. The growing popularity of loans for this purpose conjures up a picture of chastened citizens tightening their belts and cannily reducing total interest charges. The picture is quite misleading. It is true enough, of course, that in taking out one large loan from a bank a person can cut down the interest he has been paying on a variety of purchases from 25 to 30 per cent to a low of 12 or 18 per cent. But this is not the reason most purchasers take out the loan. In actual practice their consolidating is a sort of check-kiting operation by which they can square themselves away for yet another round of commitments. When these are halfway digested, they will be back again. And again.
They pay dearly for the convenience. Consider, for example, a possible alternative. A mythical couple we will call the Frugals decide to defer all but necessary purchases for enough months to accumulate an extra $500. They will then have a revolving fund of their own which they can use for cash purchases, and instead of paying out a fixed amount each month in instalment loans, they will use these sums to replenish the $500.
Now let's take a normal couple. The Joneses, with precisely the same income, don't put off purchases but instead commit themselves to a combination of instalment loans and revolving-credit plans. At the end of ten years the Joneses would have paid out somewhere around $800 in interest. The Frugals, by contrast would have earned interest -roughly $150. Not counting the extra benefits

they would have reaped by being able to buy for cash, they would be, in toto, almost a thousand dollars better off.
The Frugals, to repeat, are somewhat mythical. Most suburbanites fail to accumulate capital to produce capital, and they fail to manipulate what capital they do have. It rarely occurs to them, for example, to use their savings as collateral in taking out a loan. Were they to do this they could frequently get an actual rate as low as 41 to 41 per cent instead of the usual 10 to 12 per cent- and their savings would still earn them the regular rate of interest.
Again I say the author is speaking of people who are well trained and educated under a formal educational system which is comparable and parallel to our own.
I am very pleased to see that the royal commission is examining this very important matter. I think what is needed in this field is first of all to have forms of finance contracts, perhaps set by statute, which will clearly set forth the cost and legal effects of merchandising under this system. So far as these forms go, I think the fine print on the back should be summarized on the front in block type so that a man who signs one will know what he is signing. For example the form should tell him that the dealer is lending him the merchandise until it is paid for. He should know that if he defaults he is still liable for the price of the goods, even if they are repossessed. It should tell him that if the goods are sold and they do not bring in an amount sufficient to cover the balance of principal and interest then he can be sued in court for the difference. Also I think it should be clearly stated on the face of the form what is the total cost of finance and other charges, shown both as a sum of money and as a percentage of the principal involved.
There are some who will say that this is a free enterprise country and that we should be very careful with the ways in which we interfere with the flow of credit, particularly as much of the manufacturing industry depends on this type of instalment purchasing. I agree with that, but it is my suggestion that free choice depends upon one having a knowledge, of the facts and factors involved, so that a rational choice can be made.
I would like to see my children and all other children across the land taught in schools about this type of financing because they will be meeting it a few years after they leave school. No boy or girl should leave grade 8 without understanding that the retailer in many ways is a financier, and of what problems the consumer can get into unless he knows something about modern day merchandise financing procedures.
Mention was made today of the work done by credit unions and figures were put on the record to show their growth from 1950 to
Small Loans Act
1960. The credit union movement has given a great service to the nation in terms of funds made available to the people, particularly in rural areas, who otherwise would not have this credit obtainable to them. However, I feel one of the greatest contributions which the credit union movement has made has been in the field of education. These organizations have been formed all across the land to bring people together to study matters such as the cost of interest, and the power of savings, and also to show them how with proper handling of their finances so much more can be obtained from a dollar bill. This work of the credit union movement has done a lot of good in the nation. The credit union movement has also pioneered a movement to have some controls set up over consumer financing. This I believe is all to the good.
I would like to conclude by saying again that I am very pleased to see a royal commission on banking and finance set up, which will be inquiring into this problem. This is another example to illustrate that the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister listen to what is said by hon. members in this house. I am proud to be one of those who have raised their voices since 1958 for an inquiry into this matter of consumer financing and interest rates.

speechtext:
Any
measure introduced in either of the two houses of parliament which tends to reduce interest rates receives pretty favourable reaction in the country, and is of interest to the people. I believe this bill will receive the same consideration. I am in favour of most of its provisions. It attempts to reduce the interest rates of loans made by the small loan companies. I know that no tears will be shed by our banks, which offer a similar service, if this bill is passed. I am fully aware of the fact that our credit unions would not be hurt; as a matter of fact they would be in favour of this bill going through.
However I realize that the people most concerned, the small loans companies, would raise a hue and cry, as they have in the past, and would say that if interest rates on small loans were reduced from 24 per cent to 12 per cent it would put them out of business.
Previous speakers on this bill have proved -and I intend to add something to that proof -that the banks are doing very well at a set rate of interest. Our credit unions are doing very well too, in spite of the fact that they give more protection and more service than even the banks, and at a lower rate of interest. If we accept the amendment incorporated in this bill and it means

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill No. C-19 I first look back to previous debates when this bill was first introduced and when the interest rate was first set at 2 per cent per month on small loans. Actually it has been in effect since 1939 on loans under $500, and from 1956 on this 2 per cent per month interest rate was allowed on loans under $300.
While I support the idea and the theme behind the bill which is before us, there are several questions that come to my mind with regard to the application of the bill. Will the bill accomplish what the mover is trying to accomplish? Why has he arrived at an interest rate of 12 per cent a year, or 1 per cent a month? This is an old question that has been raised in previous debates but never really answered by the mover of this bill. He has introduced the bill several times but he has never really answered this question; therefore it remains to be answered for anyone questioning the feasibility of the bill.
The other question that I wonder about is this: what is the number of loans made every year which this bill will affect; in other words, how big or how small is the scope of this particular bill? How much money is involved, and what percentage is the money involved compared to all loans made under the Small Loans Act? This bill only sets out to reduce the interest rate on the amount of money on a loan of less than $300 so it is actually a proposal involving only a small amount. It does not cover some of the questions which have bothered me with regard to lending money in recent years; these are mainly connected with credit buying. Actually this bill does not affect loans concerning the sale of goods. In other words, T. Eaton and all the

large chain stores can continue to charge their own interest rates or debit accounts with fixed charges with regard to collection and so on. So I ask: would this bill accomplish the things I would like to see accomplished for the small people who buy goods on time?
I know that in my own home area we are not served by large chain stores to any great extent. Perhaps for this reason I do not usually take advantage of charge accounts, but since coming to Ottawa I have had occasion to make purchases in some of the large stores here, and whenever I have presented cash the clerks seemed slightly annoyed. They seemed to be thinking: why bother with this stuff-put it on the account. I wondered why they wanted me to run up a charge account, and the only conclusion I could reach was that they wanted to make money on my money; in other words they wanted to make more money on my purchases. So far they have not been too successful.

speechtext: Bankers instead of merchants.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE MAXIMUM INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River says, bankers instead of merchants. That, in a sense, is true. But with regard to the amount of money concerned in this measure, we should ask ourselves: are the interest rates too high? Are loan companies making profits that are beyond reason or exorbitant? I do not support the hon. member for Assiniboia in the attitude he has taken in the past with regard to profits. I think people and companies should be allowed to make profits. In this case we must ask ourselves whether the profits are unreasonable. The mover of this bill has not yet produced any evidence which, in my opinion, suggests that the profits are out of line. I have gone back through previous reports and I notice that in 1946 the government of the day introduced an amendment to this act to reduce the interest rate from 2 per cent to 1J per cent. This amendment was referred to the banking and commerce committee following second reading and I imagine it was given exhaustive study by that committee, though I have not had time to look up the records. In any case, the bill was not reported back to the house. Even in that year, 1946, it was stated that the companies were not charging the maximum allowable rate of interest but that they were only charging 1J per cent. However, the measure was not reported back to the house, so I am still in doubt as to whether this figure of 12 per cent
Business of the House or 1 per cent per month which the hon. member has put forward is appropriate or just in the light of all the circumstances.
I certainly support the contention that people taking advantage of small loans should be able to get them at a reasonable rate. I also recognize that when a small sum is borrowed the fixed charges may be as much as they would be on a larger loan and that therefore it is reasonable to expect that the percentage charged would be slightly higher in the case of a small loan than in the case of a larger one.
Today more than ever before we are living in a credit economy. Credit is a very important thing. In fact, I think it the most important thing. I believe that all young people going out into the world should take their credit very seriously. Actually, this bill can only affect those companies which are licensed and which have a federal charter. Loan companies or finance companies with provincial charters can operate within a province and charge any rates they like on loans above $1,500. This is a point which I should like to see covered; I think it would be more beneficial to the borrowers than the particular piece of legislation we have before us because there are a large number of people who borrow sums larger than $1,500. Many people borrow money from finance companies to purchase automobiles and other goods which are necessary in the modern world.
